# Canon: run-alloy

How run-alloy runs the Alloy analyzer, and why. It is the canon of the package `@bigmistqke/run-alloy`. Each package of this repository that runs the analyzer runs it through run-alloy. They are the Alloy plugin of the canon checker, and the test suites of naturalloy and parse-alloy. So one number of processes and one folder of kept answers serve them all.

## Terms

### @term caller

> A caller is a program that runs the Alloy analyzer through run-alloy.

The Alloy plugin of the canon checker is one, and so is each test suite of this repository that asks the analyzer.

### @term program

> A program is what the analyzer reads in one process. It is the text of a module with its commands, its path, and the files beside it that the module may open.

### @term answer

> An answer is what a [caller](#term-caller) makes of one process of the analyzer on a [program](#term-program). It may be the receipt, the text of an instance, or the lines that the analyzer printed.

### @term kept-answer

> A kept answer is an [answer](#term-answer) that run-alloy wrote to a file of its own, named by a hash of what decides it.

## @axiom the-analyzer-takes-only-the-time-its-new-programs-need

> A [caller](#term-caller) of the Alloy analyzer waits no longer than the machine that runs it needs to answer the [programs](#term-program) that no earlier run answered.

A project asks the analyzer after each change. The Alloy plugin checks a canon, and a test suite checks a parser or a verbalizer. Each program starts the analyzer anew. A program over a model of a thousand lines takes about twelve seconds on its own. A check that takes minutes gets run less often, and a defect then stays in the project for longer.

Most programs of a run ask what an earlier run asked already: a change to one unit or one formula changes few of them. So the time a run costs should follow what changed, and the machine should not lose time to processes that only wait for each other.

#### @spec the-analyzer-runs-no-more-processes-at-once-than-the-machine-holds

> By default, run-alloy runs no more analyzer processes at once than the machine has processors and memory for.

This follows because processes beyond what the machine holds start no sooner: they share the processors and the memory, and each one takes longer. Take a machine with 8 processors and 8 GB of memory. There the searches of the Alloy plugin's canon took 124 seconds with 8 processes at once, and 76 seconds with 4.

The count holds within one Node process. Two callers that run side by side, such as two test files in two workers, each count their own processes.

##### @spec the-analyzer-runs-no-more-processes-at-once-than-the-machine-has-processors

> By default, run-alloy runs no more analyzer processes at once than the machine has processors.

This follows because a process of the analyzer keeps one processor busy from start to end. A second process on the same processor only takes turns with the first.

##### @spec the-analyzer-runs-no-more-processes-at-once-than-half-the-memory-holds

> By default, run-alloy runs no more analyzer processes at once than half of the machine's memory holds at the largest heap of each.

This follows because the processes must not crowd each other, or the rest of the machine, out of memory. A machine that runs out of memory swaps, and then every process waits. The other half stays free for the system, the caller and the programs beside it.

##### @spec the-analyzer-runs-at-least-one-process

> run-alloy runs at least one analyzer process, whatever the machine has.

This follows because a caller that could start no process would get no answer. A small machine is slow, but it still answers.

##### @spec each-analyzer-process-takes-a-heap-of-at-most-one-gigabyte

> Each analyzer process that run-alloy starts runs with a heap of at most one gigabyte.

Derives from: [`fact-a-java-process-may-grow-its-heap-to-a-quarter-of-the-memory`](#fact-a-java-process-may-grow-its-heap-to-a-quarter-of-the-memory)

This follows because only a heap with a limit lets run-alloy count the processes that memory holds. Without one, four processes could take the whole memory. One search of the Alloy plugin's canon at scope 6 peaks at about 200 MB. A gigabyte leaves room for a model several times that size.

#### @spec canon-alloy-jobs-sets-how-many-processes-run-at-once

> When `CANON_ALLOY_JOBS` holds a number above zero, run-alloy runs that many analyzer processes at once, in place of the default.

This follows because the author can know a load that the machine does not show yet. A test runner may run several callers at once, and other programs may share the machine.

#### @spec a-program-asked-of-the-same-analyzer-keeps-its-earlier-answer

> run-alloy gives a [program](#term-program) the [answer](#term-answer) that an earlier run kept for it, when four things are the same as for that run. They are the program, the content of the jar, the options, and the major version of Java.

Derives from: [`fact-the-program-and-the-analyzer-decide-the-answer-of-a-search`](#fact-the-program-and-the-analyzer-decide-the-answer-of-a-search)

This follows because nothing outside those four decides the answer. A kept answer is then the answer that the analyzer would give again, and the caller need not wait for it.

The program holds the text of the module, its path and every file beside it. A change to a module it opens changes the program too. The options are those of Java, those of the analyzer, and the name of the form in which the caller reads the answer.

##### @spec an-unchanged-program-is-answered-without-the-analyzer

> When an earlier run kept an [answer](#term-kept-answer) for a program, and none of the four things changed, run-alloy starts no analyzer process for that program.

This follows because the kept answer is the one the process would give, and the process costs seconds.

##### @spec a-changed-program-is-asked-again

> When the text of a program differs from that of every kept answer, run-alloy asks the analyzer about the program.

This follows because a different model or a different command can have a different answer.

##### @spec a-program-whose-files-beside-it-changed-is-asked-again

> When a file beside a program differs from that of the run that kept an answer, run-alloy asks the analyzer again.

This follows because the module may open the file, and then the file is part of the model.

##### @spec a-program-with-another-analyzer-jar-is-asked-again

> When the content of the analyzer's jar differs from the jar that gave a kept answer, run-alloy asks the analyzer about the program again.

This follows because another version of the analyzer can translate or solve the same program in another way. The content tells two versions apart even where their paths are the same.

##### @spec a-program-with-other-options-is-asked-again

> When a caller asks about a program with other options than the run that kept an answer, run-alloy asks the analyzer again. Another form of reading the answer counts as other options.

This follows because the options decide what the answer holds. The Alloy plugin reads the text of an instance only for a scenario that `--show` names. An answer kept without that text has none to print.

##### @spec a-program-on-another-major-version-of-java-is-asked-again

> When the analyzer runs on another major version of Java than the one that gave a kept answer, run-alloy asks the analyzer again.

This follows because the analyzer runs on the Java that the caller names, and another major version is another platform.

##### @spec an-analyzer-that-did-not-answer-keeps-no-answer

> When the analyzer writes no receipt for a program, or the caller reads its process as a failure, run-alloy keeps nothing for the program. The next run asks the analyzer again.

Derives from: [`fact-the-analyzer-writes-a-receipt-only-when-it-ran-the-commands`](#fact-the-analyzer-writes-a-receipt-only-when-it-ran-the-commands)

This follows because a failure says nothing about the program. It comes from the machine or the setup, such as a missing Java or a process out of memory. The next run may not share it.

#### @spec the-folder-of-the-kept-answers-is-the-first-one-named

> run-alloy keeps the answers in the first folder of these that is named: the folder the project sets, the folder `CANON_ALLOY_CACHE_DIR` names, and the caller's default.

This follows because one folder lets every caller reuse what an earlier run answered, of any caller and any project. The program and the analyzer alone decide an answer, so callers that share a folder can share their answers. A continuous integration then saves and restores one folder for them all.

##### @spec a-folder-the-project-sets-holds-the-kept-answers

> When the project sets a folder for the kept answers, run-alloy keeps them in that folder, also when `CANON_ALLOY_CACHE_DIR` names another.

This follows because a setting that a project writes down is more particular than the environment of a run. The path of the jar and of Java follow the same order: a path in the frontmatter wins over `CANON_ALLOY_JAR` and `CANON_JAVA`.

##### @spec canon-alloy-cache-dir-holds-the-kept-answers-when-the-project-sets-none

> When the project sets no folder and `CANON_ALLOY_CACHE_DIR` names one, run-alloy keeps the answers in the folder that `CANON_ALLOY_CACHE_DIR` names.

This follows because the environment of a run names one folder for every caller at once. The callers in temporary projects keep their answers there too, which would go with the project otherwise.

##### @spec the-callers-default-folder-holds-the-kept-answers-when-none-is-named

> When neither the project nor `CANON_ALLOY_CACHE_DIR` names a folder, run-alloy keeps the answers in the caller's default folder. A caller with no default keeps none.

This follows because each caller knows where its project keeps caches. A caller with no project, such as a function that a test calls, keeps nothing that no one asked for.

##### @spec canon-alloy-cache-0-keeps-no-answer-and-reads-none

> When `CANON_ALLOY_CACHE` is `0`, run-alloy neither reads a kept answer nor keeps one, and asks the analyzer about every program.

This follows because the author may want the analyzer's own answer. The author may time the analyzer, or rule out the cache when a result looks wrong.

#### @spec the-kept-answers-are-only-those-used-in-the-last-thirty-days

> When a caller sweeps the folder of [kept answers](#term-kept-answer), run-alloy removes each kept answer that no run has used in the last 30 days.

Derives from: [`spec-a-program-asked-of-the-same-analyzer-keeps-its-earlier-answer`](#spec-a-program-asked-of-the-same-analyzer-keeps-its-earlier-answer)

This follows because a change to a model leaves the answers of its old programs behind, and no run asks them again. Without a limit, the folder grows with every change, and the author has to clear it by hand. A limit by age holds the answers that recent runs used, of every caller and every project that shares the folder. A continuous integration that saves the folder after each run saves it at that size.

##### @spec a-kept-answer-unused-for-thirty-days-is-removed

> When no run has used a kept answer in the last 30 days, the next sweep removes it.

This follows because nothing asked that program for a month, so it most likely belongs to a model that changed.

##### @spec a-kept-answer-that-a-run-uses-is-kept-for-thirty-more-days

> When run-alloy gives a program a [kept answer](#term-kept-answer), that answer counts as used at that time.

This follows because a caller that still asks the program still needs that answer, no matter how long ago the analyzer gave it.

## @fact a-java-process-may-grow-its-heap-to-a-quarter-of-the-memory

> A Java process whose command line gives no `-Xmx` may grow its heap to a quarter of the machine's memory.

The JVM sets the largest heap from the memory of the machine, by `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`, which is 25 by default. The [documentation of the `java` command](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/man/java.html) gives the default.

## @fact the-program-and-the-analyzer-decide-the-answer-of-a-search

> Whether the Alloy analyzer finds an instance for a run depends only on the program and on the analyzer. The analyzer is its jar, its options, and the Java that runs it.

A program states a model and a run within a scope, and the run has an instance or has none, whatever machine solves it. The analyzer decides it by translating the program and solving the result. The jar, its options and the Java decide that translation and that solving.

## @fact the-analyzer-writes-a-receipt-only-when-it-ran-the-commands

> `java -jar alloy.jar exec` writes `receipt.json` into its output folder only when it read the module and ran its commands. When it cannot read the module, it writes none.

Alloy 6.2.0 behaves this way. A module with a name it cannot find exits with code 1 and leaves no output folder. A module whose command it cannot translate, such as one with a higher-order quantifier, still gets a receipt. The analyzer ran the command, and said why it could not solve it.
